clinicalPearls: Mucormycosis is a group of life-threatening infections caused by fungi of the order Mucorales (subphylum Mucoromycotina); it is highly invasive and relentlessly progressive, with morbidity/mortality higher than many other infections (Harrison 22e p.1717).

Rhizopus oryzae and R. delemar (family Mucoraceae) are by far the most common causes in the Western Hemisphere; Apophysomyces elegans is a notable cause in India and Mucor irregularis in China (Harrison 22e p.1718).

Five well-defined clinical syndromes: rhino-orbital-cerebral, pulmonary, cutaneous, gastrointestinal, and disseminated; specific host defects predispose to specific syndromes (diabetes/DKA to rhino-orbital-cerebral; leukemia/HSCT to pulmonary) (Harrison 22e p.1718).

Rhino-orbital-cerebral disease is the most common form worldwide; early symptoms are nonspecific (eye/facial pain, facial numbness) progressing to conjunctival suffusion, blurry vision, proptosis, and chemosis (Harrison 22e p.1718-1719).

Biopsy with histopathology is the most sensitive and specific modality: wide (>=6-30 microm), thick-walled, ribbon-like, ASEPTATE hyphae branching at RIGHT angles, in contrast to thinner, septate, acute-angle-branching Aspergillus/Fusarium/Scedosporium (Harrison 22e p.1719).
Mucorales are best visualized with periodic acid-Schiff or H&E; methenamine silver may NOT stain them optimally (Harrison 22e p.1719).

Tissue for culture should be cut into sections and placed in the center of culture media, NOT homogenized, because homogenization kills the long filamentous hyphae and lowers culture yield; the lab should be alerted when mucormycosis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.1720).

It is important to distinguish mucormycosis from aspergillosis because treatments differ: polyenes for Mucorales versus expanded-spectrum triazoles for most septate molds; voriconazole is the first-line treatment for aspergillosis but EXACERBATES mucormycosis in animal models (Harrison 22e p.1719-1720).
harrison.pathophysiology: Mucorales are ubiquitous environmental fungi to which humans are constantly exposed; they cause invasive, angioinvasive infection primarily in hosts with uncontrolled diabetes, phagocytic defects (neutropenia or high-dose corticosteroids), and/or elevated free iron, which supports fungal growth in serum and tissue. Iron-overloaded end-stage renal failure patients treated with the iron chelator deferoxamine had high risk of rapidly fatal disseminated disease, because deferoxamine acts as a fungal xenosiderophore that delivers iron directly to the Mucorales. In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), acidosis dissociates iron from sequestering proteins (enhancing fungal survival/virulence) and the ketoacid beta-hydroxybutyrate upregulates host and fungal receptors that increase fungal adherence and tissue penetration; however the majority of diabetic patients with mucormycosis are NOT acidotic on presentation. Even without acidosis, hyperglycemia raises risk via hyperglycation of iron-sequestering proteins, upregulation of the host receptor GRP78 (which binds Mucorales and enables tissue penetration), poorly characterized phagocytic defects, and enhanced expression of the Mucorales-specific invasin CotH (which binds GRP78). Blood vessel thrombosis and tissue necrosis impair antifungal penetration to the site of infection. (Harrison 22e p.1717-1718)
additionalDifferentials: Bacterial orbital cellulitis / cavernous sinus thrombosis (Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, gram-negative species)
infectionMimics: Aspergillosis (septate mold, may co-infect with Mucorales)
Bacterial orbital cellulitis / cavernous sinus thrombosis (S. aureus, streptococci, gram-negatives)
nonInfectiousMimics: Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (painful ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, headache, cavernous sinus inflammation; lacks progression)
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy with histopathologic examination (most sensitive/specific; PAS or H&E staining)
Culture from a sterile site (needle aspirate, tissue biopsy, pleural fluid) for definitive species identification; tissue sectioned NOT homogenized, incubated at both room temperature and 37C
CT of the chest (best method to define extent of pulmonary disease; may detect infection before chest x-ray)
MRI of head/sinuses (more sensitive ~80% than CT for orbital and CNS extension)
Endoscopy and/or surgical exploration with biopsy of suspected areas; blind biopsy of normal-appearing sinus tissue when suspicion is high
Mucorales-specific PCR (useful but no FDA-approved assay)
redFlags: Rhino-orbital-cerebral involvement with a black necrotic eschar and/or painful necrotic ulceration of the hard palate (late finding indicating extensive, well-established angioinvasive infection) is a surgical emergency requiring urgent debridement.
Bilateral proptosis, chemosis, vision loss, and ophthalmoplegia (contralateral eye involvement) suggest cavernous sinus thrombosis and are ominous.

Hyperglycemia or DKA with sinusitis and possible orbital extension, even without a known diabetes history, should raise high suspicion (presentation may be the first recognition of diabetes, often unmasked by recent glucocorticoids).
Necrotizing fasciitis from cutaneous mucormycosis (mortality approaching 80%) and necrotic skin lesions from hematogenous dissemination.
Disseminated disease (most lethal form), seen with antifungal prophylaxis breakthrough and in highly immunocompromised patients.
harrison.prognosis: Overall mortality remains high though it has declined with earlier initiation of effective antifungal therapy; outcome is often driven by progression of the underlying predisposing condition. Necrotizing fasciitis from cutaneous disease carries mortality approaching 80%, gastrointestinal disease progressing to perforation has extremely high mortality, and widely disseminated disease exceeds 90% mortality. In contrast, isolated nonnecrotizing cutaneous mucormycosis treated with prompt aggressive surgical debridement has a favorable prognosis and low mortality. Rate of progression is highly variable (days to a year or more), not invariably rapid. (Harrison 22e p.1717-1720)
pitfalls: Misperception that mucormycosis is always rapidly progressive; rate of progression is in fact highly variable (days to a year or more).
Cultures are positive in fewer than half of cases, and up to half of cases are diagnosed only at autopsy; a negative culture does NOT exclude the diagnosis.
Standard tissue homogenization for culture kills the filamentous Mucorales and lowers yield; tissue must be sectioned and not homogenized, and the lab alerted.
Imaging underestimates disease: sinus CT may look like ordinary bacterial sinusitis, and bony erosion into the orbit is rarely seen on CT even when clinically present.

Treating with voriconazole (first-line for aspergillosis) can exacerbate mucormycosis; distinguish the two molds because preferred treatments differ, and consider dual infection in highly compromised patients.

Delaying treatment of the underlying malignancy until mucormycosis is 'cured' is a common error; antifungals provide only a holding action until near-normal immunity is restored, and untreated underlying disease is the typical primary driver of death.
Iron administration and liberal blood transfusion (free iron from hemolysis) should be avoided as iron exacerbates infection.
Therapy should not be delayed for diagnostic confirmation: when suspicion is reasonable, empirical lipid polyene therapy should be started early because earlier polyene therapy improves survival.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison classifies mucormycosis by clinical syndrome rather than a numeric severity score: rhino-orbital-cerebral, pulmonary, cutaneous (ranging from isolated nonnecrotizing cutaneous disease with favorable prognosis to necrotizing fasciitis), gastrointestinal, and disseminated/miscellaneous disease, with mortality rising steeply from localized cutaneous disease to disseminated disease (>90%). (Harrison 22e p.1718-1720)
